Ca2+ ions, in the micromolar range, inhibit the ATPase activity of actin in the absence of salts, and that the inhibitory effect of Ca2+, in the absence of Mg2+, is reversed by KCl, but not by NaCl.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of micromolar Ca 2+ concentrations on ATP hydrolysis by actin, and on the polymerization of muscle G-actin.
the influence of Ca2+ ions on the ATPase activity of actin and the polymerization state of actin in the presence and absence of Mg2+.
the effect of Ca2+, Mg2+ and K+ on actin ATPase activity and actin polymerization during sonication.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ATPase activity of actin is stimulated by Ca2+ in the presence of K+, and inhibited by Ca2+ under other conditions.

Ca2+ has a dual effect on actin: it stabilizes F-actin at high and labilizes F-actiin at low Ca2+ concentrations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Ca2+ is an important regulator of ATPase activity and of actin polymerization in muscle.
ATPase activity and actin polymerization in solution are interdependent.
Ca2+ is a dual regulator of actomyosin ATPase activity, i.e., it can activate or depress ATPase activity depending on the concentration of free Ca2+.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ca2+ is a powerful tool for regulating actin assembly, and that the effect of Ca2 on actin assembly is dependent on the presence of other ions such as Mg2+ and K+.
